newsitem.title: SPAIN: BT gives Telefonica big competitive edge.
newsitem.headline: BT gives Telefonica big competitive edge.

text.p: Spain's Telefonica, which last week joined British Telecommunications in a global strategic partnership, is now seen as almost unstoppable on its home turf when the telecoms market is fully liberalised in 1999.

Analysts say the BT deal took a potentially formidable contender off the playing field and dealt a heavy blow to the prospects for Spain's second basic telephone service provider Retevision, which is being auctioned off in August.
"I see Retevision's task as pretty difficult," Alberto Elosin of Madrid brokers Ibersecurities said. "BT is a strongman in Europe, giving Telefonica a lot more strength to confront competition."
Most analysts see Retevision getting only a 10 to 20 percent share of Spain's basic telephone market, which represents about 50 percent of Telefonica's total revenues, by the year 2000.
BT, which will exchange $454 million shares with Telefonica to bolster their partnership, set itself up in Spain eight years ago with the aim of becoming the country's second main provider.

The British flagship positioned itself as a competitor in data transmission through a joint venture with Spanish bank Santander and in cellular phones with a stake in Airtouch -led mobile phone group Airtel.

BT even flirted briefly about a year ago with the idea of bidding for Retevision, but said privately at the time that it had serious doubts about the state broadcaster's ability to compete with Telefonica's well-developed networks.
On Friday, BT, which is merging with U.S.-based MCI, announced with great fanfare that Telefonica had opted to become a partner rather than competitor.
The move was criticised in the Spanish media at the weekend as a sell out to foreigners, but Telefonica's chairman Juan Villalonga defended it as a necessary defensive technique.
"The alliance is an opportunity not a threat," he said in an interview with newspaper El Pais on Monday.

"The unstoppable globalisation process in telecommunications forced us to change our strategic view. We needed a very strong ally with the knowledge and financial strength to help us to get stronger in the Spanish speaking market."
Analysts agreed that BT was a good hedge against the other foreign operators who might dip into Spain's underdeveloped market by teaming up with Retevision.

"With BT backing it, Telefonica has nothing to worry about at home, even if Retevision finds a strong European partner like France Telecom or Deutsche Telekom," a Madrid-based analyst with a foreign investment house said.

Three groups put their markers down on Monday for Retevision, which becomes Spain's second basic operator by year end, giving official notice of interest for the controlling 60 percent stake the state is selling.
Italy's telecoms provider STET joined Spanish electricity groups Endesa and Union Fenosa, and Basque group Euskatel in one bid offer.
They were followed by a widely expected bid from a consortium led by Spain's BCH bank which also groups France Telecom, Deutsche Telekom and U.S. Sprint.
Retevision said that Germany's Mannesmann AG, the second mobile phone operator in Germany, also wants to make an offer -- a surprise entry for many in the market.
Telefonica shares soared to a record high at 3,655 pesetas on Monday after hitting a record on Friday after the BT/MCI deal was announced.
